81: Hill introduces the story of the United States Steel Corporation's formation in 1900 as a perfect illustration of how IDEAS convert into huge fortunes. He lists six fundamental facts demonstrating the application of the 13 Steps: First, U.S. Steel was born in Charles M. Schwab's mind as an IDEA created through IMAGINATION. Second, he mixed FAITH with his IDEA. Third, he formulated a PLAN for transforming the idea into physical and financial reality. Fourth, he put his plan into action with his famous speech at the University Club. Fifth, he applied PERSISTENCE and firm DECISION until full execution. Sixth, he prepared the way with a BURNING DESIRE for success. Hill states this story should dispel any doubt that individuals can THINK AND GROW RICH, as it plainly shows application of a major portion of the 13 Steps. The story was dramatically told by John Lowell in the New York World-Telegram. On December 12, 1900, about eighty of the nation's financial nobility gathered at the University Club on Fifth Avenue to honor a young man from the West—not half a dozen realizing they would witness the most significant episode in American industrial history.
82: The dinner was arranged by J. Edward Simmons and Charles Stewart Smith to introduce 38-year-old Charles M. Schwab to eastern banking society, after receiving lavish hospitality from Schwab in Pittsburgh. They warned Schwab that New York's stuffed shirts wouldn't respond to oratory and he should limit himself to 15-20 minutes of polite vaporings. Even J.P. Morgan, sitting at Schwab's right, intended to stay only briefly. The press found the affair so insignificant that no mention appeared in print the next day. The guests ate through seven or eight courses with little conversation—few bankers had met Schwab, whose career flowered along the Monongahela. But before the evening ended, they and Money Master Morgan were swept off their feet, and a billion-dollar baby—the United States Steel Corporation—was conceived. No record of Schwab's speech was ever made, though he repeated parts later at Chicago bankers' meetings and from the witness stand during the Government's dissolution suit. It was probably a 'homely' speech, somewhat ungrammatical, full of epigram and wit, but with galvanic force upon the five billions of estimated capital represented by the diners.
83: After the speech, Morgan led Schwab to a recessed window where they talked for another hour. Schwab's personality was turned on full force, but more important was the full-fledged, clear-cut program he laid down for steel's aggrandizement. Many had tried interesting Morgan in a steel trust—John W. Gates (the gambler, whom Morgan distrusted), the Moore brothers (Bill and Jim, Chicago stockjobbers), and Elbert H. Gary (a sanctimonious country lawyer who wasn't big enough). Until Schwab's eloquence took Morgan to heights from which he could visualize the most daring financial undertaking ever conceived, the project was regarded as a delirious dream of easy-money crackpots. The financial magnetism of combining small companies had already produced the American Steel and Wire Company (by Gates), the Federal Steel Company (Gates and Morgan), National Tube and American Bridge companies (Morgan concerns), and the Moore Brothers' 'American group' (Tin Plate, Steel Hoop, Sheet Steel, National Steel). But beside Andrew Carnegie's gigantic vertical trust—owned by 53 partners—these combinations were picayune. They couldn't dent Carnegie, and Morgan knew it.
84: Carnegie knew it too. From Skibo Castle in Scotland, he viewed the attempts of Morgan's smaller companies with amusement, then resentment. When attempts became too bold, Carnegie's temper became anger and retaliation—he decided to duplicate every mill his rivals owned. Previously content selling raw steel, he now planned to drive enemies to the wall with Schwab as his chief lieutenant. In Schwab's speech, Morgan saw the answer: a trust without Carnegie would be 'a plum pudding without the plums.' Schwab's speech carried the inference that the vast Carnegie enterprise could be brought under Morgan's tent. He talked of the world future for steel, reorganization for efficiency, specialization, scrapping unsuccessful mills, concentrating on flourishing properties, economies in ore traffic and overhead, and capturing foreign markets. He told the buccaneers their errors: creating monopolies, raising prices, and paying fat dividends from privilege. Schwab condemned this, arguing that cheapening steel's cost would create an ever-expanding market with more uses devised and world trade captured. He was, though unknowingly, an apostle of modern mass production.
85: After the dinner, Morgan went home to think about Schwab's predictions. Schwab returned to Pittsburgh to run steel for 'Wee Andra Carnegie.' It took Morgan about a week to digest the feast of reason. When ready, he sent for Schwab, who was coy—Carnegie might not like his president flirting with the Emperor of Wall Street. John W. Gates suggested a 'coincidental' meeting at the Bellevue Hotel in Philadelphia, but Morgan was ill at his New York home, so Schwab went to Morgan's library. Some economic historians believed Carnegie staged the entire drama, but the truth was opposite—Schwab didn't even know whether Carnegie would listen to an offer to sell. Schwab brought six sheets of copper-plate figures in his own handwriting, representing the physical worth and potential earning capacity of every steel company he deemed essential. Four men pondered these figures all night: Morgan (steadfast in the Divine Right of Money), Robert Bacon (aristocratic partner, scholar and gentleman), John W. Gates (whom Morgan scorned as a gambler and used as a tool), and Schwab (who knew more about making and selling steel than any group then living). Schwab's figures were never questioned—if he said a company was worth so much, it was. He insisted on including only concerns he nominated, leaving out larger concerns Wall Street had eyed, to avoid duplication.
86: When dawn came, Morgan rose and asked: 'Do you think you can persuade Andrew Carnegie to sell?' Schwab replied: 'I can try.' Morgan said: 'If you can get him to sell, I will undertake the matter.' The question remained whether Carnegie would sell, for how much (Schwab thought $320 million), and in what form of payment—nobody could raise a third of a billion in cash. In January, on the frost-cracking heath of St. Andrews links in Westchester, Carnegie bundled in sweaters and Schwab talking volubly played golf. No business was mentioned until they sat in the Carnegie cottage. With the same persuasiveness that hypnotized eighty millionaires, Schwab poured out promises of retirement comfort and untold millions. Carnegie capitulated, wrote a figure on paper, handed it to Schwab: 'All right, that's what we'll sell for.' The figure was approximately $400 million—Schwab's $320 million plus $80 million representing increased capital value over two years. Later on a trans-Atlantic liner, Carnegie told Morgan ruefully: 'I wish I had asked you for $100 million more.' Morgan replied: 'If you had asked for it, you'd have gotten it.'
87: The announcement caused uproar. A British correspondent cabled that the foreign steel world was 'appalled.' President Hadley of Yale warned that unless trusts were regulated, the country might expect 'an emperor in Washington within twenty-five years.' Stock manipulator Keene shoved the new stock at the public so vigorously that all excess water—estimated by some at nearly $600 million—was absorbed instantly. Carnegie got his millions, the Morgan syndicate got $62 million for its 'trouble,' and all the 'boys' from Gates to Gary got their millions. The 38-year-old Schwab was made president of the new corporation and remained in control until 1930. Hill explains this story perfectly illustrates DESIRE transmuted into physical equivalent. The giant organization was created in one man's mind—his FAITH, DESIRE, IMAGINATION, and PERSISTENCE were the real ingredients. The steel mills acquired after legal existence were incidental. The appraised value of properties increased an estimated $600 million by the mere transaction of consolidation. Schwab's IDEA plus the FAITH with which he conveyed it was marketed for approximately $600 million profit—not insignificant for a single IDEA.
88: Hill emphasizes that what happened to individuals who took their share of millions is not the concern—the important feature is that the story serves as unquestionable evidence of the philosophy's soundness, as it was 'the warp and woof of the entire transaction.' U.S. Steel prospered, employed thousands, developed new uses for steel, and opened new markets, proving the $600 million profit was earned. Hill declares: 'RICHES begin in the form of THOUGHT! The amount is limited only by the person in whose mind the THOUGHT is put into motion. FAITH removes limitations!' He reminds readers that Schwab was practically unknown—merely Carnegie's 'Man Friday'—until he gave birth to his famous IDEA, after which he quickly rose to power, fame, and riches. He rose on the wings of FAITH, which can be created by AUTO-SUGGESTION, transitioning to Chapter 3.
89: This page opens Chapter 3: AUTOSUGGESTION—The Medium for Influencing the Subconscious Mind (The Third Step to Riches). Hill defines autosuggestion as applying to all suggestions and self-administered stimuli reaching the mind through the five senses. It is self-suggestion—the agency of communication between the conscious thinking mind and the subconscious mind's seat of action. Dominating thoughts permitted in the conscious mind (negative or positive) reach and influence the subconscious through the Law of Autosuggestion. Critically, NO THOUGHT can enter the subconscious without autosuggestion's aid, except thoughts picked up as 'flashes of insight or inspiration.' All sense impressions perceived through the five senses are captured by the conscious mind and may be passed to the subconscious or rejected at will—the conscious faculty serves as an outer guard. Nature has wired humans with ABSOLUTE CONTROL over material reaching the subconscious through the five senses, though most people do NOT exercise this control.
90: Hill explains that failure to exercise control over subconscious input explains why so many go through life in poverty. He recalls the metaphor of the subconscious as a fertile garden where weeds grow abundantly if desirable seeds aren't sown. Autosuggestion is the agency through which one voluntarily feeds the subconscious creative thoughts, or by neglect permits destructive thoughts to enter. He references the six action steps from Chapter 1—particularly the instruction to read aloud twice daily the written statement of DESIRE FOR MONEY and to SEE AND FEEL oneself ALREADY in possession. This communicates the object of DESIRE directly to the subconscious in absolute FAITH. Through repetition, one voluntarily creates favorable thought habits. This procedure is not restricted to monetary gain—it works for whatever one DESIRES STRONGLY, so long as it doesn't violate God's laws or others' rights. Hill instructs readers to review the six actions from Chapter 1 and the Master Mind Group instructions from Chapter 6, noting all involve the Law of Autosuggestion. He warns that mere reading of words is of NO CONSEQUENCE unless mixed with emotion or feeling. Repeating Emile Coué's formula 'Day by day, in every way, I am getting better and better' a million times without emotion and FAITH produces no results—the subconscious acts ONLY upon thoughts well-mixed with emotion or feeling.
